title: Nexus
subtitle: A Brief History of Information Networks from the Stone Age to AI
author: Yuval Noah Harari
lead: Information connects people more than it informs them. Stories and documents let networks grow huge, but they create order more readily than truth.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Harari asks why a species that calls itself wise is so self-destructive. In 100,000 years Sapiens have gained enormous power, yet they now face ecological collapse, AI that may escape human control and the risk of a new world war. Old fables, from Phaethon to Goethe's Sorcerer's Apprentice, warn against summoning powers we cannot control, but they blame individual hubris and offer no answer except waiting for a god or a sorcerer to save us.

The book's main argument is that power always comes from cooperation in large numbers, and that the way large networks are built predisposes them to use power unwisely. This is a network problem, and more precisely an information problem. Information is the glue of networks, and it often binds people with fictions, fantasies and mass delusions. Nazism and Stalinism were among the most powerful networks in history, and they were held together by deeply deluded ideas.

Two views of information mislead us. The naive view, the semi-official creed of the computer age, holds that more information leads to truth, and truth to power and wisdom. It proved right about child mortality, but today every smartphone holds more information than the Library of Alexandria, and humanity is closer than ever to destroying itself. The populist view treats information as a weapon and power as the only reality; it ends by trusting a single leader. The book explores the space between these views.

AI raises the stakes because it is the first technology that can make decisions and create new ideas by itself. One danger is a Silicon Curtain that divides rival human powers; another is a curtain that divides all humans from AI overlords. History is not deterministic, so informed choices can still prevent the worst.

items.title: The Sorcerer's Apprentice
items.text: In Goethe's 1797 poem an apprentice enchants a broom he cannot stop, until the sorcerer returns. Harari notes that no sorcerer will save us.

items.title: Goethe's children
items.text: Only three of Goethe's family's 12 children reached adulthood. By 2020, 95.6% of children worldwide passed their 15th birthday, thanks to medical data.

items.title: Worried experts
items.text: In a 2023 survey of 2,778 AI researchers, more than a third gave at least a 10% chance of outcomes as bad as human extinction.

screens.label: Recap
paragraphs: Harari defines information by what it does, not by whether it is true. A star, a window shutter or a pigeon becomes information in the right context. Astrology, music, DNA and the Bible shaped history by connecting people or things, not by representing reality accurately.

So information is what puts things in formation and creates new networks. Truth, an accurate account of some aspects of reality, is rare and costly; without special effort, more information swamps it.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Harari looks at information in history rather than seeking a universal definition. Almost anything can be information in the right context: a star, a window shutter for a spy ring, a carrier pigeon for a besieged battalion. The naive view holds that something is information when it represents reality, and that information therefore leads to truth.

The book accepts that truth means an accurate account of reality, but stresses that truth is not reality itself. No account can capture every aspect of reality, just as a map at a scale of one to one would be no map at all. Truth always draws attention to some aspects and ignores others, though some accounts are more truthful than others.

Most information, however, does not represent anything. Astrology has had a huge historical impact; music synchronises people without being true or false; DNA does not describe a lion's body but helps produce it. The Bible contains serious errors about human origins and disease, yet it has connected billions of people. Errors, lies and fictions are information too. What all information does is connect things: it puts them in formation and so creates new realities.

Rejecting the naive view does not mean rejecting truth or embracing the populist view. Truthful information is rare and expensive, while fiction is cheap, so more information alone tends to swamp the truth. History shows a constant rise in connectivity without a matching rise in truthfulness or wisdom: Nazi race theory and Stalinist class theory helped tens of millions march together. The next chapter turns to the first information technology, the story.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Sapiens rule the world because they alone can cooperate flexibly in unlimited numbers. Humans cannot form intimate bonds with more than a few hundred people, but about 70,000 years ago Sapiens began to tell and believe fictional stories. A story works as a central connector: millions can link to it without knowing each other. Charismatic leaders and brands are crafted stories of this kind, and shared stories can even give strangers common memories, as the Passover ritual does.

Before stories there were two levels of reality: objective (stones, asteroids) and subjective (pain, love). Stories add a third, intersubjective reality: laws, gods, nations, corporations and money, which exist in the communication between many minds. The calories in a pizza are objective, but its price is intersubjective. A state exists if enough people agree that it does.

Story-based networks made Sapiens the most powerful animal, and identities such as nations and religions are always intersubjective, not just masks for material interests. Since history is shaped by stories, new stories and talk can also avert conflict.

Power depends on truth and on order. Those who keep order usually command those who know the truth: physicists obey politicians and theologians. Fiction has two advantages: it can be simple, and it can be comforting where truth is painful. Plato proposed a noble lie to justify hierarchy. A third option is a fiction that admits it is one, like the US Constitution, which can be amended; the Ten Commandments claim divine origin and cannot be. Every network walks a tightrope between truth and order, and faster information technology makes the balance more urgent.

items.title: Two pizzas for 10,000 bitcoins
items.text: Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas in 2010; by November 2021 they were worth about $690m. The value was intersubjective.

items.text: A 2021 study found headquarters knew the battalion's position before the pigeon arrived; the heroic story was partly a branding campaign.

items.title: The Manhattan Project

chapters.title: Documents: The Bite of the Paper Tigers

screens.label: Recap
paragraphs: Stories inspire nations, but states run on lists of taxes and debts, which brains remember poorly. Writing solved this, and documents created new realities: ownership, debt and citizenship came to depend on paper.

Finding documents needed bureaucracy, which sorts the world into drawers and trades some truth for order. It traced cholera and built sewers, but people distrust it because it fits none of the biological dramas our minds understand.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Nations are often first imagined by poets and dreamers, as Bialik and Herzl imagined a Jewish nation, but dreams alone cannot run a state. Armies need taxes and cities need sewers, and such services run on lists of property, payments and debts. Stories are easy to remember and lists are not, so complex taxation needed a non-organic technology: the written document. Lists and stories complement each other: myths make tax records legitimate, and tax records turn stories into schools and hospitals.

Documents can be wrong, as a clay tablet from Ur with a miscounted total shows, but they also create new realities. In oral communities ownership rested on the neighbours' agreement; in a literate state the document decides, and a distant authority can hold it. In old Assyria a debt died with its contract.

Writing created a new bottleneck: finding the right document. Bureaucracy is the order devised to solve this problem. It divides the world into drawers and forces people to fit its forms, and narrow goals in separate drawers can cause harm, from polluting officials to academic disciplines that ignore what falls between them. Even biology's species are conventions, yet a label such as endangered species can decide life or death.

Bureaucracy also does great good. John Snow's lists of cholera cases traced an epidemic to one water pump, and sewage systems, the real deep state, save millions. Because bureaucracy does not follow the biological dramas that our minds and our art understand, people find it hard to grasp and easy to suspect. It can also destroy lives, as a 1938 Romanian law did to Harari's grandfather. AI is now taking over the roles of both bureaucrats and mythmakers.

items.title: John Snow, 1854
items.text: By listing cholera patients and their water sources, Snow traced London's outbreak to the Broad Street pump, less than a metre from a cesspit.

items.title: Bruno Luttinger
items.text: Harari's grandfather lost his Romanian citizenship in December 1938, with 367,000 of 758,000 Romanian Jews; he escaped to Palestine in 1940.

items.title: Clean India
items.text: From 2014 to 2020 India's Clean India Mission spent about $10bn and built more than 100 million latrines.

items.title: Kafka's Trial
items.text: Art handles death by a tiger well but death by a document poorly; Kafka's novel is one of the few works about a faceless bureaucracy.

questions.a: Taxation and services run on lists, which brains remember badly, so lists had to be stored outside the brain.

questions.a: It does not follow the biological dramas our minds and stories are built for, so it seems faceless and suspect.
